content: Flu season refers to the predictable annual increase in influenza cases that typically occurs during the colder months of the year. The onset of flu activity varies by geographic location, but in any given area, these localized outbreaks generally take about three weeks to reach their peak and another three weeks to significantly decline. However, individual cases of influenza usually last only a few days. In some countries, such as Japan and China, individuals infected with the flu may wear surgical masks as a courtesy to prevent spreading the virus to others. Influenza is responsible for approximately 36,000 deaths and over 200,000 hospitalizations annually. The seasonal flu is caused by influenza viruses A, B, or C, which are collectively referred to as human flu virus strains. These viruses have undergone genetic adaptations to infect human hosts effectively. Influenza viruses circulate among humans year-round and never completely disappear. However, during colder months, infections caused by human flu viruses increase significantly, often by tenfold or more. The flu virus is constantly mutating, leading to the emergence of different strains each year. The influenza vaccine for the 2005–2006 flu season, for example, contained proteins derived from the viral coat of two subtypes of influenza A and one strain of influenza B. Unlike influenza A, species B and C do not have subtypes. The reasons for the seasonal nature of flu outbreaks remain unclear. One hypothesis is that people spend more time indoors during the winter, leading to closer contact and increased transmission. Another theory suggests that cold temperatures result in drier air, which may dehydrate the mucus lining of the respiratory tract, impairing the body’s ability to expel virus particles effectively. Additionally, the virus may survive longer on exposed surfaces, such as doorknobs and countertops, in colder conditions. Increased travel and social gatherings during the holiday season may also contribute to the spread of the virus. Flu vaccinations are a key strategy in mitigating the impact of flu season. Since the Northern and Southern Hemispheres experience winter at different times of the year, there are two distinct flu seasons annually. To address this, the World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with National Influenza Centers, develops two separate vaccine formulations each year—one for the Northern Hemisphere and one for the Southern Hemisphere. Many large companies now offer seasonal flu vaccinations to their employees, either at a reduced cost or free of charge. The annually updated trivalent influenza vaccine contains hemagglutinin (HA) surface glycoprotein components from influenza H3N2, H1N1, and B viruses. As of January 2006, the dominant circulating strain was H3N2. However, resistance to standard antiviral drugs such as amantadine and rimantadine in H3N2 has risen dramatically, from 1% in 1994 to 12% in 2003, and further to 91% in 2005.
